If a finite set $I$ of parameter directions has its own fitted potential bounds $n^{(i)}$, this definition is $D(n^{(0)})+\sum_{i\in I}\bar\varrho_iD(n^{(i)})+w_*^{-1/2}\{[\sum_{i\notin I}\bar\varrho_i^2/\varpi_i]^{1/2}(n_{\mathrm v}+n_{\mathrm d})+[\sum_{i\notin I}|\varsigma_i|\bar\varrho_i]n_\theta\}$. The paper-specific identification sets $I=\varnothing$, leaving the first two terms of (B.53). The constraint replacement charge is added separately. The definition itself accepts arbitrary real inputs and takes division by zero to be zero and the square root of a negative real number to be zero; its application requires $w_*>0$ and $\varpi_i>0$, and nonnegative norm bounds. It is a proposed numerical budget, with no assertion here that the fields satisfy it.

This definition forms $n_\Phi+n_Yc_\Xi/\sqrt{w_*}$. Here $n_\Phi$ bounds $\|\sum_lY_{jl}(\Phi_l-\widetilde\Phi_l)\|_{\mathcal H}$, $n_Y$ bounds the Euclidean norm of the row $(Y_{jl})_l$, and $c_\Xi$ controls the $L^2$ matrix error in replacing $\Xi_l$ by $\nabla\Phi_l$. The two contributions pair with $\Delta v$ and $\nabla v$ respectively. For a positive constant weight they give the last part of (B.53) after division by the energy norm. This declaration defines the number; the assertions that it bounds those pairings, and that the indicated numbers bound the norms, are separate statements. Division by zero is defined to be zero, but the intended use has $w_*=39/50>0$.

For the fixed adjoint $\psi_j$, compact generators $\widetilde\Phi_l$ and real coefficients $Y_{jl}$, this definition forms $K=

abla\widetilde\Phi_l-(

For the divergence-free generators of the paper, $-\operatorname{div}K=-\Delta\psi_j+\sum_lY_{jl}\Delta\widetilde\Phi_l$, which supplies precisely those terms in (B.52). notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded: Let $R$ be a measurable real vector field on $\mathbb R_\theta\times\mathbb R_y^3$, and let $n\ge0$. The condition represents each of $R_1+iR_2$, $R_1-iR_2$ and $R_3$, almost everywhere in $y$ for every $\theta$, as a finite sum $\sum e^{2\pi i k'\theta}g(y)$. Each amplitude is measurable and satisfies $g(R_\phi y)=e^{ik\phi}g(y)$ for every angle and point. The integers $k',k$ are distinct as pairs within each component. It requires $\sum c\,(|k|+1/2)^{-2}\int|y|^2|g|^2\le n^2$, with $c=1/2$ for each horizontal complex component and $c=1$ for the third. The denominator is positive for every integer $k$, including zero. The representation implies period one almost everywhere; exact pointwise periodicity is not a separate assumption. These are the harmonic terms called $R''$ in the paper's dual bound.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.I: For real vectors $v,R\in\mathbb R^3$, define $v^+=v_1+iv_2$, $v^-=v_1-iv_2$ and $v^0=v_3$, and use the same convention for $R$. The formal statement proves $v\cdot R=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\overline{v^+}R^+)+\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\overline{v^-}R^-)+v_3R_3$. This is an identity of real numbers, with no regularity or integrability hypotheses. It is the component decomposition used at the end of the proof of Lemma B.11. The two horizontal factors are $1/2$; the vertical factor is $1$. The formal component labels begin at zero and refer in order to $+$, $-$ and the vertical component.

For any real matrix $M:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, let $M^+$, $M^-$ and $M^0$ be the matrices obtained by taking the two horizontal rows as a complex pair, its conjugate, and the vertical row. The formal statement proves $\tfrac12|M^+|^2+\tfrac12|M^-|^2+|M^0|^2=|M|^2$, where each squared norm is the sum of the squared absolute values of its entries, and the complex pair is represented by its two real coordinates. Taking $M=\nabla v$ gives the weighted gradient identity in the proof of Lemma B.11. The formal theorem is purely algebraic for every matrix; applying it almost everywhere and integrating gives the same identity for any weakly differentiable field with finite gradient energy. No symmetry, periodicity or solenoidality is assumed.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.g: For a measurable matrix field $G:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, the formal statement proves that the sum over all integer azimuthal modes of its gradient energy in the rotating cylindrical frame is at most $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|G|^2$. The mode energy is integrated with cylindrical measure $2\pi r\,dr\,dz$ on $r>0$, $z\in\mathbb R$; the matrix norm on the right is the sum of squares of all entries. Both sides are nonnegative extended integrals. The statement applies to any measurable matrix field, without requiring that it be the derivative of a velocity. This is the spatial Fourier-energy estimate used to pass from single-mode inequalities to the total bound. Projection in the time variable is a separate operation.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m: Let $v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and its weak gradient $G$ be measurable, with $v\in L^6$ and $G\in L^2$. Put $U=v_1+iv_2$, and let $U_k(r,z)$ be its normalized angular Fourier coefficient. Given the smooth azimuthal estimate, approximation by smooth compactly supported fields in gradient norm and local $L^2$, and the bound of the total Fourier gradient energy by $\int|G|^2$, the formal statement proves $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(|k|+1/2)^2\,2\pi\int_{r>0,z\in\mathbb R}r|U_k|^2/(r^2+z^2)\,dr\,dz\le\int|G|^2$. Thus it controls all angular projections together. The paper states (B.50) for a single complex field already having wave number $k$; representing that field by two real components yields its special case. The three analytic premises are supplied by separate proved declarations in the formalisation. No divergence or reflection assumption on $v$ occurs.

Let $u,B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C$ be measurable, and assume $B(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi,z)=e^{ik\phi}B(r,0,z)$ for an integer $k$. Let $u_k(r,z)$ be the angular coefficient normalized by $1/(2\pi)$. The formal statement gives $|\int\overline{u}B|^2\le[2\pi\int_{r>0,z\in\mathbb R}r|u_k|^2/(r^2+z^2)]\,[\int|y|^2|B|^2]$. This uses Cauchy–Schwarz after angular projection; combining it with the azimuthal Hardy estimate produces the factor $(|k|+1/2)^{-1}$ in the paper. The displayed conclusion uses the opposite complex conjugation from the paper's pairing, which has the same absolute value. There is no hypothesis that the ordinary complex integral on the left exists in the analytic sense. If its integrand is not integrable, that integral is assigned the value zero. The right-hand side uses nonnegative integrals, which may equal infinity. Thus this statement alone does not establish integrability of the pairing. In the application, finite weighted bounds and a separate integrability theorem justify its ordinary analytic interpretation.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.s: Let $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth with compact support, and let $U=u_1+iu_2$. For any integer $k$, form the angular coefficient $U_k(r,z)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{-ik\phi}U(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi,z)\,d\phi$. The formal statement bounds $(|k|+1/2)^2\,2\pi\int_{r>0}\int_{\mathbb R}r|U_k(r,z)|^2/(r^2+z^2)\,dz\,dr$ by the corresponding Fourier component of the full gradient energy, represented in the rotating cylindrical frame. It is a statement about an angular projection of a smooth real vector field. Taking $u=(\operatorname{Re}U,\operatorname{Im}U,0)$ when $U$ already has wave number $k$ gives the smooth scalar inequality in (B.50). Extending to an $L^6$ field with a weak $L^2$ gradient requires the separate approximation result. The denominator is nonzero on $r>0$.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.t: Take a finite family of measurable complex amplitudes $a_p(y)$ and distinct integer temporal frequencies $k'_p$. The formal statement proves $\int_0^1\int|y|^2|\sum_p e^{2\pi i k'_p\theta}a_p(y)|^2\,dy\,d\theta\le\sum_p\int|y|^2|a_p(y)|^2\,dy$. Both sides are nonnegative extended integrals. The frequencies need be distinct only on the selected finite index set. In the adjoint proof this is applied separately to groups having the same azimuthal order, for which distinct pairs imply distinct temporal frequencies. Its conclusion is a weighted $L^2$ estimate for finite harmonic sums; the paper's displayed Bessel inequality concerns arbitrary space-time projections in gradient norm.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.w: Let a measurable vector field $v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ have measurable weak gradient $G$, with $v\in L^6$ and $\int|G|^2<\infty$. There exists a sequence of smooth compactly supported real vector fields $u_n$ such that $\int|\nabla u_n-G|^2\to0$ and, for every real radius $R$, $\int_{B_R}|u_n-v|^2\to0$. The ball is centered at the origin; for negative $R$ it is empty. A specified azimuthal wave number is preserved by the subsequent angular projection, which is a separate step. The conclusion here is the approximation before that projection. Complex scalar functions are handled by their real and imaginary parts. No solenoidality condition is required.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.DualBounded: A real field $R$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ has this bound $n$ when it is the pointwise sum of two measurable fields $R_h+R_p$, with nonnegative bounds $n_h,n_p$ satisfying $n_h+n_p\le n$. The first derivative decay bound is also in operator norm; (7.8) uses the Frobenius norm, and conversion at a fixed constant costs at most $\sqrt3$. The weight is measurable, bounded above and below by positive finite constants, and invariant under the spatial isometries of the prescribed symmetries. The coefficient $c_2$ is explicitly nonnegative. Each adjoint field has a common spatial $L^2$ bound at every time, in addition to periodicity. The residual is a specified expression using a supplied measurable periodic vector field whose pairing with compact solenoidal tests vanishes. No scalar pressure is supplied by this hypothesis; the paper allows a residual specified only modulo gradients. The integer used in the supremum estimate may be $1$, or $2$ if a half-period symmetry is present; the paper's convention (7.6) chooses $2$ whenever such a symmetry is available. All coefficient and residual norms, positivity conditions and inequalities (7.18)–(7.37) are assumptions in the corresponding formal certificate, subject to these encodings.
